summary: Defines the architecture of Netnews systems and how software that creates, distributes, stores and displays articles should treat them. It also sets requirements for any protocol that transports or serves Netnews articles.

plainLanguage.summary: Netnews distributes articles among servers that accept, relay, store, or display them. RFC 5537 defines what each kind of software does and how it helps prevent duplicate articles, unwanted changes, and gateway loops.

subtitle: Define how Netnews articles move between servers, moderators, gateways, and readers.

tldr.problem: Netnews distributes copies of articles among many servers without a central authority. Shared rules are needed to reject duplicates, preserve article contents, and limit loops or abuse.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns duties to posting, injecting, relaying, serving, moderation, and gateway agents, and defines transport requirements, article history, Path tracing, media types, and control messages.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5537 obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849. RFC 8315 later updates it, and the RFC notes that control-message authentication is not standardized.

today: RFC 5537 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2009. It obsoletes RFC 1036 and RFC 1849, and the unit metadata says RFC 8315 updates it.

sections.title: The Netnews System
sections.content:
Netnews is a set of protocols for creating, storing, retrieving, and exchanging articles organized into newsgroups. Servers commonly use flooding: each server offers articles to peers, and each server stores a copy and serves it to readers.

Usenet is one public network using Netnews protocols; other deployments also exist. This RFC describes the general architecture and transport requirements. The article format is specified separately in RFC 5536.
sections.plainLanguage: Netnews articles are copied between servers and grouped by topic. Readers retrieve articles from a server that stores them.

sections.title: The Software Roles
sections.content:
A posting agent helps a person prepare an article and gives it to an injecting agent. An injecting agent accepts it and starts distribution. Relaying agents pass accepted articles to peers, and serving agents store articles and make them available to reading agents.

Moderators review articles for moderated newsgroups. Gateways convert articles to or from another medium, such as email, or connect separate Netnews networks. One software package may perform several server roles and must meet the requirements for each role.
sections.plainLanguage: Different agents prepare, inject, relay, store, and display articles. Moderators approve articles for moderated groups, and gateways translate between Netnews and other systems.

sections.title: Posting and Injecting an Article
sections.content:
A posting agent creates a proto-article, which may omit Message-ID, Date, or Path. It MUST NOT add Injection-Info. If a posting agent offers the same article to multiple injectors, the copies must have the same Message-ID, Date, and Injection-Date.

The injecting agent checks article syntax and required headers, adds missing Message-ID and Date fields, and MUST NOT change the body. It adds or updates Path and SHOULD add Injection-Info. For a moderated group without an Approved field, it sends the article to the moderator or rejects it.
sections.plainLanguage: A posting agent can leave certain headers for the injector to fill in. The injector checks the article, adds missing fields, and does not alter the article body.

sections.title: Path Tracing and Duplicate Suppression
sections.content:
Every injecting, relaying, or serving agent prepends its identity to the article's Path header. The path is assembled from right to left. A diagnostic can show whether the agent verified the previous server's identity, found a mismatch, or merely recorded that it saw the article.

Because flooding can deliver the same article from several peers, relaying and serving agents MUST keep an article history and reject repeats by Message-ID. For Usenet, a cutoff of no less than seven days is conventional. An agent may avoid sending an article to a peer whose identity is already in the Path.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server adds its identity to Path, creating a trace of the article's route. Servers also remember Message-IDs so they can reject another copy of an article they already accepted.

sections.title: Moderation and Gateways
sections.content:
A moderator decides whether to approve a proto-article. If it is approved for all moderated groups, the moderator adds an Approved header and passes it to an injecting agent. Moderators may modify an article, but the RFC recommends making only necessary changes.

Gateways must prevent the same message from being reinjected repeatedly. An incoming gateway creates a valid proto-article, adds a Sender field for the gateway administrator, and passes the article to an injecting agent. The RFC recommends preserving message identifiers and using other checks to prevent loops between email and newsgroups.
sections.plainLanguage: A moderator approves an article before it enters a moderated group. A gateway must recognize messages it has already converted so they do not circulate repeatedly.

sections.title: Article Transport and Control Messages
sections.content:
The transport is not fixed; NNTP is common, and the RFC also names UUCP and physical media. A transport treats an article as uninterpreted octets, must not carry NUL, and must preserve CR LF as the line separator. It must convey header fields unchanged.

A control message has a Control header requesting an action, such as creating or removing a group, checking a group list, or cancelling an article. The RFC registers three media types for transmitting articles and group information. A control message is only a request; each server may decide whether to act on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Different transports can carry articles, but they must preserve article headers and line endings. Control messages request server actions, but servers are not required to honor them.

sections.title: Security and Distribution Risks
sections.content:
Netnews provides little security beyond the underlying transport. If servers cannot authenticate peers, articles can be forged and widely distributed, and sender identity and privacy cannot be assured.

Control messages are especially sensitive because they can remove groups or articles or create groups. No standardized authentication method exists for them, so agents SHOULD authenticate according to local policy. Article contents must be treated as untrusted. The flooding method can also carry restricted articles beyond an intended network boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Without trusted transport, a sender can be impersonated and an article can be altered or forged. Servers should check control messages before acting because they can change groups or remove articles.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1036
sections.content:
The RFC updates the Path format, requires References-header trimming, and defines when posting and injecting agents add an Injection-Date. It also introduces media types for article transmission and control-message information.

Several old control messages are declared obsolete, the subject text cmsg no longer identifies a control message, and the old message/news media type is obsolete. The RFC also formalizes many steps that earlier Netnews servers already performed.
sections.plainLanguage: This version documents new tracing and date rules and adds structured formats for articles and group information. It also removes special meaning from an old subject-line convention.
